extracted.intended_audience: USPTO design patent examiners and patent practitioners preparing/responding to design patent filings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of design patent applications addressing amendments, written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a)), definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b)), and restriction practice for multiple embodiments. Covers when amendments introduce new matter, how to evaluate written description support (drawings as the disclosure), claim definiteness, and when restriction is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments must not introduce new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim may be amended by broadening or narrowing its scope within the bounds of the disclosure as originally filed provided it complies with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). An amendment to the claim which has no support in the specification and/or drawings as originally filed introduces new matter because that subject matter is not described in the application as originally filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (A) An amendment changing the configuration of the original design by the addition of previously undisclosed subject matter introduces new matter (In re Salmon). (B) Changing surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed three-dimensional surface treatment (beading, grooves, ribs) is new matter. By contrast, removal of two-dimensional, superimposed surface treatment will not introduce new matter if it is clear the underlying configuration was possessed at filing. Converting originally-disclosed solid lines to broken lines (or vice versa) will not introduce new matter where no new elements are added, but any amendment affecting the claimed design must be evaluated for written description compliance. Preliminary amendments filed with application papers and inclusion of disclaimers in original specification/drawings/photographs are examples of amendments that would not introduce new matter. (See MPEP §§ 1504.04, 1503.02, 608.04(b); 37 CFR 1.121(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings define scope; drawings satisfy written description for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a design claim is defined by what is shown in full lines in the application drawings. For designs, 'it is the drawings of the design patent that provide the description of the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Contessa Food Prods. v. Conagra; Daniels. If features are not desired to be claimed they may be shown in broken lines to exclude them; failure to do so signals inclusion. The written description test is the same for design and utility patents (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description sufficiency test (possession standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for sufficiency of written description is whether the disclosure of the application relied upon reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (Ariad). 'Possession as shown in the disclosure' and 'the hallmark of written description is disclosure.' For ornamental designs, the practical question is whether earlier illustrations depict the later-claimed ornamental design (Racing Strollers). The analysis is from the perspective of an ordinary designer; courts have emphasized whether a skilled artisan would recognize the claimed portion as separable or claimable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate amended claims and priority/continuation claims for written description support
rubrics_metrics.description: A written description issue generally involves whether the subject matter of a claim is supported by the disclosure of an application as filed. This question arises when an amended claim is presented or when a claim for priority/benefit of an earlier-filed application is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A continuation must comply with the written description requirement to be entitled to the parent application's filing date (Owens; Daniels). If the later-claimed design is not reasonably conveyed by the earlier disclosure, the claim should be rejected for lack of written description and will not be entitled to the earlier date (see MPEP §§ 1504.10, 1504.20). Examples: Munchkin v. Luv N’ Care (spout shape not specifically disclosed) illustrates failure to convey possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the resulting amended design as a whole for written description compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When an amendment affects the claimed design, the resulting amended design must be evaluated for compliance with the written description requirement; the fact that an amendment only affects features that were originally disclosed does not negate the need to determine whether the amendment complies with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if elements of the later-claimed design are individually visible in the original disclosure, additional consideration may be required to determine whether the whole later-claimed design was reasonably conveyed to an ordinary designer. In many cases (e.g., converting solid/broken lines) the examiner can determine possession by reviewing drawings; in limited situations further analysis is required. If not reasonably conveyed, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (see Ariad, Daniels, Racing Strollers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record must be clear; examiner must set forth basis and consider applicant submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner determines that an amendment to a design claim is not supported by the original disclosure, the examiner should set forth a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the next Office action, specifically identifying the differences or changes made to the claimed design that are not supported in the original disclosure. The Office has the initial burden of establishing a prima facie case for any rejection and must set forth express findings of fact supporting that rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a general statement that the amended drawing/specification/title contains new matter. When repeating a rejection after applicant response, review the basis in view of the record as a whole (amendments, arguments, affidavits/declarations). If the record demonstrates written description is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If again rejecting, fully respond to rebuttal arguments and properly treat applicant's evidence (In re Alton). Use form paragraphs such as ¶15.51 (35 U.S.C.112(a) rejection) and ¶15.65 where appropriate. Examiner notes in form paragraphs advise specifying what is unsupported and suggesting corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application may be fatally defective if definite enabled claim cannot be identified without new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If an amendment that introduces new matter into the claim is the result of a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) and it is clear that the disclosure as originally filed cannot support any definite and enabled design claim without the introduction of new matter, the record of the application should reflect that the application is seen to be fatally defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 15.65 may be used to set forth this position. In bracketed text, identify the subject matter which is insufficiently disclosed. This signals that applicant may have no viable way to obtain a valid claim absent new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b)) evaluated in light of disclosure and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects in claim language give rise to a rejection under the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The definiteness of the language employed must be analyzed not in a vacuum but in light of the teachings of the prior art and of the particular application disclosure as it would be interpreted by one possessing the ordinary level of skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim may appear indefinite in the abstract but be definite when read with the application disclosure or prior art (In re Moore). There is no per se rule; evaluate facts and circumstances of each application. Use form paragraphs 15.22 and 15.22.02 for 'or the like' style problems. Use ¶15.22.03 when title fails to specify a known article of manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening language in title: 'or the like' / 'or similar article' cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of phrases in the claim such as 'or similar article,' 'or the like,' or equivalent terminology has been held to be indefinite. However, the use of broadening language in the title when directed to the environment of the article embodying the design should not automatically be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C.112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Pappas held such phrases indefinite in some contexts. Examiner notes: ¶15.22.02 should be used where there is another rejection in the Office action; do not use when phrase in the title is directed to the environment of the article. ¶15.69.01 may be used to remove indefinite language by examiner's amendment (with appropriate authorization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title must identify a known article of manufacture or request additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be rejected as indefinite when it cannot be determined from the designation and the drawing what article of manufacture is being claimed (e.g., 'widget' that does not identify a known or recognizable article). If the title of the article is too ambiguous, the examiner should request additional information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶15.22.03: reject when title fails to specify a known article of manufacture; clarifying the title by specifying the article may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C.132 and 37 CFR 1.121). ¶15.21.01 requests applicant to provide a sufficient explanation of the nature and intended use of the article, and additional helpful information (analogous fields of search, prior art, brochures, co-pending utility application numbers). Submit information as separate paper, not inserted in specification (37 CFR 1.56; 1.97; 1.98).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction practice: single claim rule and when to require restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application may only have a single claim (37 CFR 1.153(a)). More than one embodiment of a design may be protected by a single claim only if they involve a single inventive concept according to nonstatutory double patenting practice for designs. The examiner will require restriction in each design application which contains more than one patentably distinct design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 if multiple designs are patentably distinct. The test for patentable distinctness requires: (A) the embodiments have overall appearances with basically the same design characteristics; and (B) the differences between the embodiments are insufficient to patentably distinguish one design from the other (differences de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill). Clear admissions by applicant that embodiments are not patentably distinct do not overcome restriction if evidence lacking. Use nonstatutory double patenting analysis (In re Rubinfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple embodiments may be included only if single inventive concept; disclose and particularize differences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to illustrate more than one embodiment of a design in a single application only if they involve a single inventive concept. The specification should make clear that multiple embodiments are disclosed and should particularize the differences between the embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure of any embodiment relies on another for completeness, the differences must be identified in figure descriptions or by a descriptive statement in the specification (example statement: 'is a second embodiment of Figure 1, the only difference being the configuration of the door, it being understood that all other surfaces are the same as those of the first embodiment'). In the absence of such statements, one embodiment's disclosure will normally not be permitted to provide antecedent basis for amendments to other embodiments. Embodiments that are patentably distinct over one another may not be included in the same application (In re Platner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction analysis uses two-step overall-appearance/obviousness test
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether multiple embodiments may be retained in a single application, first determine whether the embodiments have overall appearances that are basically the same. If so, determine whether the differences are minor/insufficient to patentably distinguish or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in view of analogous prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embodiments meet both criteria, they may be retained in a single application. If embodiments do not have basically the same overall appearances, restriction must be required regardless of obviousness. If overall appearances are the same but differences are not obvious or are patentable distinctions, restriction is required. A prior-art search may be necessary to resolve these questions. Form paragraphs 15.27.02 or 15.27.03 may be used to notify applicant that restriction is not required when appropriate.
